title: Toad in the Hole
subtitle: Pork sausages baked in golden Yorkshire pudding batter
excerpt: Whole pork sausages cooked in a hot, lard-greased tin and covered with Yorkshire pudding batter that puffs and crisps around them. An old British bake, unchanged for centuries.
sourceNotes: Eliza Acton, Modern Cookery for Private Families (1845), batter pudding with meat documented. Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), Project Gutenberg #10136, toad in the hole listed as a recipe for inferior cuts baked in batter. The name first appears in print in the eighteenth century. By the Victorian era, sausages were the standard filling.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the batter up to 1 hour ahead and leave at room temperature. Do not refrigerate.

glossaryTerms.definition: Leaving batter to rest after mixing allows the gluten in the flour to relax and the starch granules to absorb the liquid. The result is a more even, reliable rise during baking.

content.text: Toad in the hole is sausages baked inside Yorkshire pudding batter. It works on the same principle as Yorkshire pudding: a wet batter poured into a tin of searingly hot fat, which rises in the oven to form a crisp, golden crust around the meat. The key rules are the same as for Yorkshire pudding: the fat must be smoking hot before the batter goes in, and the oven door stays shut until the batter is set.

Make the batter: whisk {{plain-flour}} of flour with {{sea-salt-fine}} of salt, then whisk in {{eggs}} eggs and enough of {{whole-milk}} of milk to make a smooth, thin batter the consistency of single cream. Rest for at least 30 minutes. This is
and it matters for the rise.
Heat oven to 220 degrees C. Put {{lard}} of lard into a large roasting tin and place in the oven for 10 minutes until the fat is smoking hot.
Add {{sausages-pork}} sausages to the hot tin and return to the oven for 10 minutes until the sausages are just starting to colour.
Working quickly, pour the rested batter all around the sausages. The fat should sizzle immediately. Return to the oven at once.
Bake for 25 to 30 minutes without opening the oven door. The batter should be deep golden and well risen around the sausages. Serve immediately with onion gravy and mustard.

rows.symptom: Batter does not rise and stays flat and stodgy
rows.cause: Fat not hot enough when batter was poured, or oven door opened during baking
rows.fix: The fat must be smoking before the batter goes in. Do not open the oven door during the first 25 minutes or the batter will collapse.

rows.symptom: Batter is soft and doughy inside
rows.cause: Oven too cool, or tin too small so batter is too deep
rows.fix: Use a large tin so the batter spreads thin around the sausages. A thin layer rises and crisps; a thick pool steams and stays doughy.

rows.cause: Poured the batter before the sausages had any colour
rows.fix: Give the sausages 10 minutes in the hot fat before adding the batter. They should have some colour on at least one side.

rows.cause: Too little fat, or wrong type of tin
rows.fix: Use enough fat to coat the base generously and ensure it is smoking. A metal roasting tin works better than ceramic or glass, which hold heat less efficiently.

content.text: Toad in the hole has been in British cookbooks since the eighteenth century, though not always with sausages: early recipes used offcuts of meat or leftover roasts embedded in batter. Victorian cookery writer Mrs Beeton listed it as a way to use inferior cuts. Sausages became the standard filling during the nineteenth century as pork sausages became more widely available and affordable. The dish belongs to a group of British batter-based puddings that includes Yorkshire pudding, clafoutis-adjacent fruit batters, and baked pancakes. It remains a standard British home dinner, particularly in the north of England.
